tasks.title: Continuous force versus discrete compounding — calibrated rates
tasks.context: A stock of capital follows the continuous model $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$ with $P_0>0$ and force $a>0$. A rival discrete model uses the same initial level but annual factor $(1+b)$ with $b>0$, namely $Q(t)=P_0(1+b)^t$. Assume throughout that $1+b\neq e^{a}$ (so the one-year multipliers disagree). Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.06$, $b=0.05$, initial level $2500$, horizon $T=8$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $t>0$, the continuous one-year multiplier equals $1+a$.
The paths $P$ and $Q$ coincide for every $t\ge 0$.
The continuous doubling time is $T=\dfrac{\ln 2}{a}$, independent of $P_0$.
Replacing $e^{at}$ by $(1+a)^t$ leaves every level $P(t)$ unchanged.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Under continuous force $a$, the one-year multiplier is $e^{a}$.

$$e^{a}\neq 1+a\quad(a\neq 0)$$

So the multiplier is not $1+a$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

Two exponential paths with the same $P_0$ agree for all $t$ if and only if their one-year multipliers match.

$$1+b=e^{a}$$

The stem assumes $1+b\neq e^{a}$, so $P$ and $Q$ diverge for $t>0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

When $b=a>0$, the inequality $e^{a}>1+a$ forces $P(t)>Q(t)$ for $t>0$, so the claimed reverse comparison fails.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Doubling means $P(T)=2P_0$, so $e^{aT}=2$.

$$T=\frac{\ln 2}{a}$$

The initial level $P_0$ cancels, so $T$ depends only on $a$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The substitution $(1+a)^t$ for $e^{at}$ changes the one-year multiplier from $e^{a}$ to $1+a$. Since $e^{a}\neq 1+a$ for $a>0$, levels move.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Recover the continuous path $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$ and the discrete rival $Q(t)=P_0(1+b)^t$. One-year multipliers are $e^{a}$ and $1+b$; they agree for all $t$ precisely when $1+b=e^{a}$. The inequality $e^{a}>1+a$ (for $a>0$) settles the $b=a$ comparison. Doubling solves $e^{aT}=2$, giving $T=\ln 2/a$.

tasks.title: Recovering continuous force from an exact sample table
tasks.context: A positive level $P$ is known to be continuous-exponential, $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$ with unknown letters $P_0>0$ and $a\in\mathbb{R}$. The table records exact values (not rounded measurements) at four integer times. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For some consecutive pair in the table, $\dfrac{P(t+1)}{P(t)}\neq e^{a}$.
The same table is also generated by the discrete model $P(t)=P_0(1+a)^t$ for every $a$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Every consecutive ratio equals $e^{a}$ identically, so the claim fails.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

At $t=0$ one has $P(0)=P_0$, and $P(1)=P_0 e^{a}$.

$$a=\ln\frac{P(1)}{P(0)}$$

That is exactly the recovered force.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Discrete growth with additive rate $a$ would use ratios $1+a$, not $e^{a}$.

$$1+a\neq e^{a}\quad(a\neq 0)$$

So the table is not generated by $P_0(1+a)^t$ for arbitrary $a$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{P(2)}{P(0)}=a$$

The recovered value is $a$, not $2a$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

If $a>0$ then $e^{3a}>e^{2a}$, so $P(3)>P(2)$. The claimed inequality is reversed.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: The table is the exact sampling of $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$. Consecutive ratios are $e^{a}$, so $a=\ln(P(1)/P(0))$ and equally $a=\tfrac12\ln(P(2)/P(0))$. Discrete $(1+a)^t$ matches only in the knife-edge case $1+a=e^{a}$.

tasks.title: Doubling and half-life identities with calibrated force
tasks.context: Let $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$ with $P_0>0$. Write $T_{2}=\dfrac{\ln 2}{|a|}$ for the doubling time when $a>0$, and $T_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln 2}{|a|}$ for the half-life when $a<0$. Both letters denote the same formula in $|a|$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.04$, $c=0.01$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: In both regimes, $T_2$ (or $T_{1/2}$) is independent of $P_0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$T_2=\frac{\ln 2}{a}$$

The factor $\ln 2$ is required; $1/a$ is not the doubling time.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$P\!\left(\frac{\ln 2}{c}\right)=P_0 e^{-c\cdot(\ln 2)/c}=P_0 e^{-\ln 2}=\frac12 P_0$$

That is the half-life identity.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

In $e^{aT}=2$ (or $e^{-c T}=\tfrac12$) the factor $P_0$ cancels before taking logs, so the characteristic time depends only on $|a|$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The linearised guess $1/a$ ignores the logarithm.

$$\frac{\ln 2}{a}\neq\frac{1}{a}$$

Exact doubling uses $\ln 2$, not $1$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

$$P(2T_2)=P_0 e^{a\cdot 2(\ln 2)/a}=P_0 e^{2\ln 2}=4P_0$$

Two doubling times multiply the level by four.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Solve $e^{aT}=2$ or $e^{-c T}=\tfrac12$ to obtain $T=\ln 2/|a|$. The initial level cancels. After two doubling times the factor is $2^2=4$.

tasks.title: Two continuous forces $a$ and $b$ — parametric comparison
tasks.context: Two positive stocks start equal: $A(0)=B(0)=S_0>0$. Thereafter $A(t)=S_0 e^{a t}$ and $B(t)=S_0 e^{b t}$ with letter forces $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $a\neqb$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.12$, $b=0.10$, initial level $1200$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $A(t)>B(t)$ for every $t>0$ if and only if $a<b$.
The crossing time where $A(t)=B(t)$ for some $t>0$ always exists.
If $a>b$, the gap $\ln A(t)-\ln B(t)$ grows linearly in $t$.
Because the starts agree, $A(t)=B(t)$ for every $t$ even though $a\neqb$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\frac{A}{B}=e^{(a-b)t}$$

The ratio exceeds $1$ for $t>0$ precisely when $a>b$, not $a<b$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

Since $A(0)=B(0)$ and $a\neqb$, the ratio $e^{(a-b)t}$ equals $1$ only at $t=0$. There is no later crossing.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$\frac{A}{B}=e^{(a-b)t}$$

The exponent uses the difference of forces, not the sum.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

$$\ln A(t)-\ln B(t)=(a-b)t$$

When $a>b$ this linear function of $t$ is strictly increasing.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Equal starts cancel in the ratio, leaving $e^{(a-b)t}$, which is not identically $1$ when $a\neqb$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: With equal starts, $A/B=e^{(a-b)t}$. Sign of $a-b$ decides which path leads for all $t>0$; unequal forces never cross again. Log-gap is exactly $(a-b)t$.

tasks.title: Rebuild $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$ from a doubling time
tasks.context: A continuous-exponential level is known to double every $T>0$ time units: $P(t+T)=2P(t)$ for every $t\ge 0$. It is also known that $P(0)=P_0>0$. No numeric census is supplied — only the letters $P_0$ and $T$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.07$, $b=0.05$, initial level $400$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rebuilt model is linear in $t$: $P(t)=P_0\bigl(1+\dfrac{t\ln 2}{T}\bigr)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Doubling on every window of length $T$ means $e^{aT}=2$.

$$a=\frac{\ln 2}{T}$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$P(t)=P_0\,2^{t/T}$$

The exponents $t/T$ and $T/t$ are not interchangeable.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The identity $e^{aT}=2$ yields $a=\ln 2/T$, not $1/T$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$P(bT)=2^b P_0$$

Doubling stacks multiplicatively as powers of two, not as $b\cdot 2\,P_0$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The linear expression is the first-order Taylor guess for $e^{(\ln 2)t/T}$, not the exponential solution of the doubling condition.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: From $e^{aT}=2$ recover $a=\ln 2/T$, hence $P(t)=P_0 e^{(\ln 2)t/T}=P_0\,2^{t/T}$. Integer multiples of $T$ produce exact powers of two.

tasks.title: Nested exponential–log compositions with letters
tasks.context: Fix letters $a>0$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}$. Consider the nested expressions $e^{b\ln a}$, $a^{b}$, $\ln(e^{bt})$, and $e^{\ln(P_0)+bt}$ with $P_0>0$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.05$, $b=0.04$, $c=0.02$, $d=0.03$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $a>0$ and every real $b$, $e^{b\ln a}=a^{b}$.
If $P(t)=P_0 e^{bt}$, then $\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+bt$ for every $t$.
The map $t\mapsto e^{b\ln(1+c)}$ with fixed $c>-1$ equals $(1+c)^{bt}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$e^{b\ln a}=\bigl(e^{\ln a}\bigr)^{b}=a^{b}$$

The identity holds for all $a>0$ and all real $b$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+bt$$

Natural log turns the continuous force into a linear trend.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$e^{\ln P_0+bt}=P_0 e^{bt}$$

Exponent sum becomes a product with $P_0$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Because $\ln$ and $\exp$ are inverses on $\mathbb{R}$,

$$\ln(e^{bt})=bt$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

$$e^{b\ln(1+c)}=(1+c)^{b}$$

There is no extra factor of $t$ in the exponent of the base-$(1+c)$ form.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Use $e^{b\ln a}=a^{b}$ and $\ln\circ\exp=\mathrm{cd}$. Continuous growth $P_0 e^{bt}$ is exactly $e^{\ln P_0+bt}$; never rewrite that as a sum.

tasks.title: Semi-log slope reads the calibrated force $a$
tasks.context: A level follows $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$ with $P_0>0$. The figure shows an illustrative semi-log plot of $\ln P$ against $t$ for one positive pair $(P_0,a)$. In the letters, the same geometry always holds. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.06$, initial level $2500$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: On the $(t,\ln P)$-plane the graph is a straight line of slope $P_0 a$.
On the $(t,\ln P)$-plane the graph is a straight line of slope $P_0$.
The intercept of that line at $t=0$ equals $\ln P_0$.
Chord slopes equal $a$ only for the special window $[0,1]$.
If $a>0$, the ordinary $(t,P)$-plot is itself a straight line.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\ln P=\ln P_0+at$$

The slope is $a$, not $P_0 a$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

The slope is the force $a$, not the initial level $P_0$. The letter $P_0$ appears only in the intercept $\ln P_0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Substitute $t=0$ into $\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+at$ to read the intercept $\ln P_0$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Because $\ln P$ is exactly linear, every chord equals $a$, not merely the unit window.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

On the raw $(t,P)$-plane one sees $P_0 e^{at}$, which is curved (convex) for $a\neq 0$, not a straight line.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Take logs once: $\ln P=\ln P_0+at$. Semi-log slope and every chord equal $a$; intercept is $\ln P_0$. The raw level plot remains exponential.

tasks.title: Tangled quantifiers on continuous exponential paths
tasks.context: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be the family of all functions of the form $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$ with letters $P_0>0$ and $a\in\mathbb{R}$. Statements below mix universal and existential claims about members of $\mathcal{E}$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.08$, $b=0.07$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: A path $P\in\mathcal{E}$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$ if and only if $a\ge 0$.
For every $P\in\mathcal{E}$ with $a\neq 0$, the equation $P(t)=2P_0$ has exactly one real root.
There exists $P\in\mathcal{E}$ such that $P(t)=P_0+at$ for every $t$.
If $P\in\mathcal{E}$ satisfies $P(t+b)=P(t)P(b)/P_0$ for all real $t,b$, then the functional equation holds automatically for every member of $\mathcal{E}$.
For every $a\in\mathbb{R}$ there is a choice of $P_0>0$ making $P(t)$ identically $1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$P'(t)=a P(t)$$

Strict increase needs $a>0$; the weak inequality $a\ge 0$ wrongly includes the constant case $a=0$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$e^{at}=2\implies t=\frac{\ln 2}{a}$$

For $a\neq 0$ there is exactly one real solution (positive if $a>0$, negative if $a<0$).

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

An exponential $P_0 e^{at}$ equals the affine path $P_0+at$ for all $t$ only in degenerate limits that fail for a fixed pair $(P_0,a)$ across every $t$. No such member exists.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Compute for any $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$:

$$\frac{P(t)P(b)}{P_0}=P_0 e^{a(t+b)}=P(t+b)$$

So Cauchy-type scaling holds for the whole family.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Identically $1$ forces $P_0=1$ and $a=0$ simultaneously. For a prescribed nonzero $a$ no choice of $P_0$ works. The universal claim over every $a$ is false.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Sign of $a$ governs monotonicity. Hitting $2P_0$ is a single log solve when $a\neq 0$. Exponentials are not affine. The multiplicative Cauchy identity holds for every $P_0 e^{at}$.

tasks.title: Piecewise continuous force — switch at letter $T$
tasks.context: A fund follows the piecewise continuous-exponential rule $$P(t)=\begin{cases}P_0 e^{a_1 t},&0\le t\le T,\\[4bt]P_0 e^{a_1 T}e^{a_2(t-T)},&t>T,\end{cases}$$ with letters $P_0>0$, $T>0$, and forces $a_1,a_2\in\mathbb{R}$ (not necessarily equal). Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.04$, $b=0.03$, initial level $5000$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $P$ jumps discontinuously at the switch time $t=T$.
If $a_1\neq a_2$, then $P$ fails to be continuous at $t=T$.
The average force on $[0,T]$ recovered from $\dfrac{1}{T}\ln\dfrac{P(T)}{P_0}$ equals $a_2$.
One may replace the whole path by the single force $a_1$ for all $t\ge 0$ without changing any value, even when $a_2\neq a_1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$P(T-)=P(T+)=P_0 e^{a_1 T}$$

The pieced definition is continuous at $T$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

Continuity at $T$ uses only the matching value $P_0 e^{a_1 T}$; it does not require $a_1=a_2$. A kink in the derivative can occur while the level stays continuous.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

For $t>T$, take logs of the second piece:

$$\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+a_1 T+a_2(t-T)$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

$$\frac{1}{T}\ln\frac{P(T)}{P_0}=a_1$$

The early window sees force $a_1$, not $a_2$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

After $T$, the true force is $a_2$. Whenever $a_2\neq a_1$ the constant-$a_1$ extrapolation disagrees for $t>T$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Match values at $T$ to keep continuity; log-linearise each piece separately. Early average force is $a_1$. A single global force $a_1$ cannot replace a genuine switch.

tasks.title: GDP per capita — force $a-b$ trap with calibrated rates
tasks.context: Aggregate real output and population follow $Y(t)=Y_0 e^{at}$ and $N(t)=N_0 e^{bt}$ with letters $Y_0,N_0>0$ and forces $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$. Per capita output is the ratio $c(t)=Y(t)/N(t)$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.12$, $b=0.10$, $c=0.05$, $d=0.08$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The continuous force on $c$ is exactly $a-b$.
The continuous force on $c$ is exactly $a+b$.
If $a>0$ and $b>0$, then necessarily $c$ is strictly increasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\ln c=\ln Y-\ln N=\ln Y_0-\ln N_0+(a-b)t$$

Differentiating (or reading the coefficient of $t$) shows the force is $a-b$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Adding forces would describe a product $YN$, not the ratio $Y/N$. The sum trap $a+b$ is not the per-capita force.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$c(t)=c_0 e^{(a-b)t}$$

Per capita carries the difference force, not the sum.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Differentiate $\ln c=\mathrm{const}+(a-b)t$ to obtain $a-b$ at every $t$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Growth of $c$ requires $a-b>0$, not merely $a>0$ and $b>0$. If population force exceeds output force, per capita falls.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Logs turn the ratio into a difference of forces: $\ln c=\ln c_0+(a-b)t$. Never add $a$ and $b$ for per capita. Sign of $a-b$ alone governs whether $c$ rises.

tasks.title: Competing populations with calibrated rates $a_A,a_B$
tasks.context: Two populations obey $A(t)=A_0 e^{a_A t}$ and $B(t)=B_0 e^{a_B t}$ with $A_0,B_0>0$ and real forces $a_A,a_B$. The figure is an illustration for one positive-rate scenario; claims stay in letters. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.07$, $d=0.09$, initial level $400$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The time at which $A(t)=B(t)$ (when it exists and is unique) solves $t=\dfrac{\ln(B_0/A_0)}{a_A-a_B}$ provided $a_A\neq a_B$ and the right-hand side is positive.
Equal initial levels $A_0=B_0$ force $A(t)=B(t)$ for every $t$, regardless of $a_A,a_B$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\frac{A}{B}=\frac{A_0}{B_0}e^{(a_A-a_B)t}\to\infty$$

The ratio diverges, rather than tending to $0$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Set $A_0 e^{a_A t}=B_0 e^{a_B t}$ and take logs:

$$t=\frac{\ln(B_0/A_0)}{a_A-a_B}$$

Whenever this $t$ is positive it is the unique crossing.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A larger start can still be overtaken when the rival force is larger. The claim that $A$ stays ahead forever is false in general.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$\frac{d}{dt}\ln\frac{A}{B}=a_A-a_B$$

The log-ratio grows at the force gap, not the sum.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Equal starts give $A/B=e^{(a_A-a_B)t}$, which stays $1$ for all $t$ only if $a_A=a_B$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Compare via the ratio $A/B=(A_0/B_0)e^{(a_A-a_B)t}$. Crossings are a single log solve; long-run leadership follows the larger force.

tasks.title: Diagnosing discrete versus continuous from a twin table
tasks.context: Two positive processes are tabulated exactly. $U$ is proposed as discrete annual compounding with letter factor $(1+b)$, $b>-1$, $b\neq 0$. $V$ is proposed as continuous force $a\neq 0$. Initial levels $U_0,V_0>0$ are letters. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.05$, $b=0.04$, initial level $1000$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The successive ratios of $U$ are constant and equal to $1+b$.
If $1+b=e^{a}$ and $U_0=V_0$, then the tabulated values still disagree at $t=2$.
Constant successive ratios are incompatible with any exponential model.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\frac{U(1)}{U(0)}=1+b,\quad \frac{U(2)}{U(1)}=1+b$$

Discrete compounding has constant ratio $1+b$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$\frac{V(t+1)}{V(t)}=e^{a}$$

Continuous force yields ratio $e^{a}$, not $1+a$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

When $1+b=e^{a}$ and starts agree, both models produce the same geometric sequence, so the $t=2$ entries match. The claim that they disagree is false.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Constant ratios are the hallmark of pure exponential (discrete or continuous) structure.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The table never equates $b$ with $a$; it only exhibits ratios $1+b$ and $e^{a}$. Those letters may differ.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Read constant ratios off each row: $1+b$ for discrete, $e^{a}$ for continuous. The models coincide on the grid precisely when $1+b=e^{a}$ and starts match — not when $b=a$.

tasks.title: Newton cooling structure with ambient letter $T_a$
tasks.context: A temperature $T(t)$ obeys Newton cooling toward a constant ambient letter $T_a$: $$T(t)=T_a+\bigl(T(0)-T_a\bigr)e^{-bt},$$ with force letter $b>0$ and $T(0)\neq T_a$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.06$, $b=0.05$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The gap $T(t)-T_a$ is a pure exponential with force $+b$.
The path $T(t)$ itself is a pure exponential $Ce^{bt}$ through the origin of temperature.
Solving $T(t)=T_\ast$ for a target between $T(0)$ and $T_a$ yields $t=\dfrac{1}{b}\ln\dfrac{T(0)-T_a}{T_\ast-T_a}$.
If $T(0)>T_a$, then $T(t)$ is increasing for all $t>0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$T(t)-T_a=\bigl(T(0)-T_a\bigr)e^{-bt}\to 0$$

Hence $T(t)\to T_a$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$T(t)-T_a=(T(0)-T_a)e^{-bt}$$

The gap force is $-b$, not $+b$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Unless $T_a=0$, the level $T(t)$ is an exponential plus a nonzero constant, not a pure through-origin exponential.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Set $T_a+(T(0)-T_a)e^{-bt}=T_\ast$ and rearrange:

$$e^{-bt}=\frac{T_\ast-T_a}{T(0)-T_a}$$

$$t=\frac{1}{b}\ln\frac{T(0)-T_a}{T_\ast-T_a}$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

When $T(0)>T_a$ the object cools toward ambient, so $T$ is decreasing, not increasing.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Rewrite Newton as an exponential gap to $T_a$. Long-run limit is ambient; hitting times are log solves on the gap. The temperature level is affine-plus-exponential, not a pure $Ce^{bt}$.

tasks.title: Matching discrete factor $(1+b)$ to continuous force $a$
tasks.context: A bank offers discrete annual growth with letter factor $(1+b)$, $b>-1$. A continuous rival uses force $a\in\mathbb{R}$. Both start at the same $P_0>0$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.08$, $b=0.07$, $c=0.03$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The two models agree at every integer year if and only if $e^{a}=1+b$.
Setting $a=b$ fails to match the models at integer years whenever $b\neq 0$.
The continuous force that matches the discrete factor is $a=\ln(1+b)$ (for $b>-1$).
For $b>0$, the matching force $\ln(1+b)$ is strictly smaller than $b$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

At integer $c$, discrete gives $P_0(1+b)^c$ while continuous gives $P_0 e^{ac}$. Equality for all $c$ holds iff $e^{a}=1+b$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Unless $b=0$, one has $e^{b}\neq 1+b$, so $a=b$ does not match discrete compounding.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$a=\ln(1+b)$$

That is the unique continuous force matching the discrete factor.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$\ln(1+b)<b\quad(b>0)$$

Strict concavity of $\ln$ yields the inequality.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

$$\ln(1+b)<b\quad(b>0)$$

The inequality goes the other way.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Equate one-year multipliers: $e^{a}=1+b$ forces $a=\ln(1+b)$. The naive $a=b$ overstates continuous force relative to discrete factor when $b>0$.
tasks.tables_markdown:
| spelling | one-year factor | continuous force |
| --- | --- | --- |
| discrete | $1+b$ | — |
| matched continuous | $e^{a}$ | $a=\ln(1+b)$ |
| naive $a=b$ | $e^{b}$ | $b$ |

tasks.title: Rebuild continuous force from two lettered observations
tasks.context: A continuous-exponential path passes through two observations $\bigl(t_1,P(t_1)\bigr)$ and $\bigl(t_2,P(t_2)\bigr)$ with $t_2>t_1$ and positive levels. Letters $P(t_c)$ stand for the observed values. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.04$, $b=0.03$, $c=0.01$, initial level $5000$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The recovered force is $a=\dfrac{\ln P(t_2)-\ln P(t_1)}{t_2-t_1}$.
The rebuilt path may be written $P(t)=P(t_1)\,e^{a(t+t_1)}$ with that $a$.
The same two points always determine a unique discrete factor $(1+b)$ that matches them at every real $t$, not merely on an integer grid.
A third off-path observation is still compatible with the same pure continuous-exponential model.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$a=\frac{\ln P(t_2)-\ln P(t_1)}{t_2-t_1}$$

That is the unique continuous force through the two points.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$P(t)=P(t_1)e^{a(t-t_1)}$$

The correct time shift is $t-t_1$, not $t+t_1$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

A discrete factor $(1+b)^t$ is not even defined the same way for non-integer $t$ without extending via $\exp(t\ln(1+b))$, which then collapses to a continuous force. There is no separate discrete path that matches two points at every real $t$ while remaining a different model.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Three inconsistent points overdetermine and reject a two-parameter exponential.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The difference quotient of raw levels is not the continuous force; force uses logs.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Two positive observations fix $a$ via a log chord and then fix the whole path by anchoring at one point. Raw slopes are not forces; a third off-path point rejects the model.

tasks.title: Rewriting $a^{t}$ as continuous force $\ln a$
tasks.context: Fix a letter base $a>0$, $a\neq 1$, and write $b(t)=a^{t}$. View $b$ as a continuous-exponential path. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.12$, $b=0.10$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$a^{t}=e^{t\ln a}$$

Definition of real exponentiation.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Force is the coefficient of $t$ in the exponent after writing $e^{(\cdot)t}$, namely $\ln a$, not the base $a$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$a^{t}=e^{t\ln a}$$

Force is $\ln a$, not the discrete net $a-1$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

$$a^{T}=2\implies T\ln a=\ln 2\implies T=\frac{\ln 2}{\ln a}$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Writing $a=1+(a-1)$ does not convert the continuous force into $a-1$. Force remains $\ln a$, while $a-1$ is a discrete one-year net rate relative to $1$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Pass to $e^{t\ln a}$ to read force $\ln a$. Doubling solves $a^{T}=2$. Do not confuse $\ln a$ with the discrete net $a-1$.

tasks.title: Hybrid — integer doubling table meets continuous force $\ln 2$
tasks.context: The table records exact levels of a continuous-exponential path at integer times. The figure sketches the same path. Treat the pattern as $P(t)=e^{at}$ with unknown letter $a$ to be recovered (here $P_0=1$). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The same table is not generated by force $a=2$.
Matching the integer grid fixes $P_0$ and $a$, so the continuous extension beyond integers is unique.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$e^{a}=2\implies a=\ln 2$$

The force is $\ln 2$, not $2$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$P(t)=e^{(\ln 2)t}=2^{t}$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

With $a=\ln 2$, doubling time is $\ln 2/a=1$, matching the table's step.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Force $a=2$ would give ratios $e^{2}$, not $2$, so it does not generate the table.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

A continuous exponential is completely determined by $P_0$ and $a$. The integer samples pin both letters, so non-integer values are determined.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Ratio $2$ forces $a=\ln 2$ and $P(t)=2^{t}$. Doubling time is $1$. The continuous extension beyond integers is unique.

tasks.title: ‘For every’ and ‘precisely when’ in exponential claims
tasks.context: Throughout, $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$ with $P_0>0$. Quantifiers range over real times and over letter parameters as written. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.05$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $a\in\mathbb{R}$, $P$ is unbounded above on $[0,\infty)$.
$P$ is unbounded above on $[0,\infty)$ precisely when $a>0$.
For every $P_0>0$ and every $a$, the identity $P(0)=2P_0$ holds.
For every $t>0$, the map $a\mapsto P(t)$ is decreasing.
The equality $P(t)=P_0$ for every $t$ holds precisely when $a=0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

If $a\le 0$ then $P$ is bounded on $[0,\infty)$ (constant or decaying). The universal claim over every $a$ fails.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

For $a>0$, $P(t)\to\infty$. For $a\le 0$ it does not. That is precisely the dichotomy.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

$$P(0)=P_0$$

The initial value is $P_0$, not $2P_0$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial a}P(t)=t P_0 e^{at}>0\quad(t>0)$$

So $a\mapsto P(t)$ is increasing in $a$, not decreasing.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

$P(t)=P_0$ for all $t$ iff $e^{at}=1$ for all $t$ iff $a=0$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Read quantifiers carefully: unboundedness needs $a>0$; constancy needs $a=0$. Partial derivatives in $a$ show larger force raises every positive-time level.

tasks.title: Piecewise growth then decay — letters $a_+,a_-$
tasks.context: A biomarker follows force $a_+>0$ on $[0,T]$ and force $-a_-$ with $a_->0$ after $T$: $$P(t)=\begin{cases}P_0 e^{a_+ t},&0\le t\le T,\P_0 e^{a_+ T}e^{-a_-(t-T)},&t>T.\end{cases}$$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.06$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The peak value on $[0,\infty)$ equals $P(T)=P_0 e^{a_+ T}$.
For $t>T$, the half-life relative to the peak is $\dfrac{\ln 2}{a_+}$.
$\ln P$ rises with slope $a_+$ before $T$ and falls with slope $-a_-$ afterward.
If $a_+=a_-$, the path is symmetric about $t=T$ in calendar time for all horizons.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Before $T$ the path rises; after $T$ it falls. Continuity at $T$ makes $P(T)$ the global peak.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

After $T$ the decay force is $a_-$, so the half-life is $\ln 2/a_-$, not $\ln 2/a_+$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$P(t)=P(T)e^{-a_-(t-T)}\to 0$$

not $P_0$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Log-linear slopes are exactly the instantaneous forces on each piece.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Equal magnitudes make the rise and fall rates match, but symmetry about $t=T$ for all horizons would also require mirroring the time domain; decay continues forever while growth only occupied $[0,T]$, so global calendar symmetry fails.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Peak at the switch, then exponential decay to $0$ with half-life $\ln 2/a_-$. Semi-log slopes flip from $+a_+$ to $-a_-$.

tasks.title: Unit trap — letter $M$ millions versus raw counts
tasks.context: A city population is reported as $M(t)$ million residents with $M(t)=M_0 e^{at}$, letters $M_0>0$ and $a\in\mathbb{R}$. The raw headcount is $H(t)=10^6\,M(t)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $H$ obeys the same continuous force $a$ as $M$.
Doubling time for $H$ is one million times the doubling time for $M$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$H(t)=10^6 M_0 e^{at}$$

A positive constant factor does not change continuous force, so $H$ still has force $a$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Doubling solves $e^{aT}=2$ for both series; the $10^6$ cancels. Doubling times coincide.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$\ln H=\ln M+\ln(10^6)$$

The raw headcount adds $\ln(10^6)$, rather than subtracting it.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Differentiating the previous display shows both semi-log slopes equal $a$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

If $M_0=3$ (millions), then $H(0)=3\cdot 10^6$, not $3$. That is the unit trap.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Changing units by a positive constant rescales the level but preserves force, doubling time, and semi-log slope. Never drop the $10^6$ when reading headcount.

tasks.title: Reading a continuous growth graph in letters
tasks.context: The figure illustrates a path of the form $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$ with $P_0>0$, $a>0$. Interpret all claims in those letters (the sketch uses one admissible pair). Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.04$, $c=0.01$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The elasticity $\dfrac{t P'(t)}{P(t)}$ equals $a$ (with no factor of $t$).
For every $c>1$ there is a unique $T>0$ with $P(T)=c P_0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$P''(t)=a^{2} P_0 e^{at}>0$$

for $a\neq 0$, so with $a>0$ the path is strictly convex.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$\frac{t P'(t)}{P(t)}=at$$

An extra factor of $t$ remains.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

$$P''(t)=a^{2} P(t)>0$$

for $a\neq 0$ and finite $t$, so $P''$ has no root.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$\frac{P'(t)}{P(t)}=a$$

that constant is the continuous force.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$T=\frac{\ln c}{a}>0$$

unique because $P$ is strictly increasing.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Differentiate $P_0 e^{at}$ to read constant relative rate $a$, positive second derivative, and unique hitting times $T=\ln c/a$ for each multiple $c>1$.

tasks.title: Equal log-increments diagnose constant force $a$
tasks.context: An analyst tabulates log-increments of a positive series $P$ over successive unit windows and finds they all equal the same letter $a$. Assume $P$ is continuous and strictly positive. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: On each integer window the continuous average force equals $a$.
The table alone proves $P$ cannot be discrete-geometric with factor $e^{a}$.
If $P$ is known a priori to be continuous-exponential, then its force equals $2a$.
Equal unit-window log-increments force $P$ to be linear in $t$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

By definition the average force on $[b,b+1]$ is the log-increment, here equal to $a$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Discrete geometry with ratio $e^{a}$ produces exactly these log-increments on the integer grid. The table does not rule that model out.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Constant unit log-increments of size $a$ identify the force as $a$, not $2a$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Chaining $b$ unit increments of size $a$ multiplies by $e^{ab}$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Equal log-increments produce exponential (or geometric) behaviour, not affine linearity.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Constant log-increments mean constant average force on each window. On the integer grid this matches both $e^{at}$ and geometric $(e^{a})^{b}$. It does not yield a line.

tasks.title: Radioactive-style decay with letter rate $c$
tasks.context: A mass follows $c(t)=c_0 e^{-c t}$ with letters $c_0>0$ and $c>0$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.07$, $b=0.05$, $c=0.02$, $d=0.09$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Time to reach fraction $b\in(0,1)$ of $c_0$ is $t=\dfrac{\ln b}{c}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$e^{-c T_{1/2}}=\frac12\implies T_{1/2}=\frac{\ln 2}{c}$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$c(d T_{1/2})=c_0 e^{-\ln 2\cdot d}=2^{-d}c_0$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$c(t)=c_0 e^{-c t}$$

Reading the exponent shows force $a=-c$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$\frac{c'}{c}=-c$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

$$t=\frac{-\ln b}{c}$$

Because $\ln b<0$, the correct expression carries a minus sign (equivalently $\ln(1/b)/c$).

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Decay force is $-c$. Half-life $\ln 2/c$ stacks as powers of $\tfrac12$. General fraction $b$ solves by the same log.

tasks.title: Per capita with growth letters $a$ and population $b$
tasks.context: Rename the earlier macro forces: output grows at letter $a$ and population at letter $b$, so $Y=Y_0 e^{a t}$, $N=N_0 e^{b t}$, and $c=Y/N$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.05$, $b=0.04$, $c=0.02$, initial level $1000$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Maximising $a$ alone always maximises the force on $c$, holding nothing else fixed in a comparative-static sense is automatic even if $b$ rises one-for-one with $a$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Same log-ratio argument as with $(a,b)$: force on $c$ is $a-b$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

When $a=b$ the force on $c$ is $0$, not $a$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

$$c(t)=c(0)e^{0\cdot t}=c(0)$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

If $b$ rises one-for-one with $a$, the difference $a-b$ is unchanged. Raising $a$ alone need not raise per-capita force when $b$ co-moves.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Integrate force $a-b$ from the initial level $c(0)$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Per-capita force is the difference $a-b$. Equal forces freeze $c$. Watch co-movement of population force when comparing policies.

tasks.title: Rebuild decay from a lettered half-life
tasks.context: A decaying continuous-exponential mass has half-life letter $H>0$ and initial mass $b_0>0$. Rebuild $b(t)$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.06$, $b=0.05$, initial level $2500$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rebuilt model has positive continuous force.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$e^{aH}=\frac12\implies a=-\frac{\ln 2}{H}$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$b(t)=b_0\,2^{-t/H}=b_0 e^{-(\ln 2)t/H}$$

Decay needs the negative exponent; the claimed positive exponent describes growth.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The positive exponent $2^{t/H}$ would describe growth, contradicting half-life decay.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

$$b(H/2)=b_0\,2^{-1/2}=b_0/\sqrt{2}$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Force $a=-(\ln 2)/H$ is negative.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Half-life $H$ means $e^{aH}=\tfrac12$, so $a=-(\ln 2)/H$ and $b(t)=b_0 2^{-t/H}$.

tasks.title: Nested form $e^{a\ln(P/Q)}$ as a relative power
tasks.context: Let $P,Q>0$ be positive letter levels and $a\in\mathbb{R}$. Study the nested scalar $e^{a\ln(P/Q)}$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.08$, initial level $800$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $a=0$, the nested expression equals $1$ for every positive $P,Q$.
The identity $e^{a\ln(P/Q)}=a\ln(P/Q)$ fails for some choices of $a\neq 0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$e^{a\ln(P/Q)}=(P/Q)^{a}$$

The base is $P/Q$, not its reciprocal.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$a\ln(P/Q)=a\ln P-a\ln Q$$

Exponentiating preserves the split.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$e^{0}=1$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$e^{a\ln 1}=e^{0}=1$$

Equal positive levels force the log argument to $1$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Exponential and identity maps agree only at special points. For example $a=1$, $P/Q=e$ gives $e\neq 1$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Collapse $e^{a\ln(P/Q)}$ to $(P/Q)^{a}$. Special cases: $a=0$ gives $1$; $P=Q$ gives $1$.

tasks.title: Hybrid — equal starts, calibrated force gap $\delta$
tasks.context: Two funds start equal, $A_0=B_0=S_0>0$, with forces $a$ and $a+\delta$ where the gap letter satisfies $\delta\neq 0$. Thus $A(t)=S_0 e^{at}$ and $B(t)=S_0 e^{(a+\delta)t}$. The figure illustrates $\delta>0$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.04$, initial level $5000$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The funds do not cross again at any $t>0$.
If $\delta>0$, then $B$ eventually dominates $A$ by an arbitrarily large factor.
The force gap $\delta$ equals $\dfrac{B(t)-A(t)}{t}$ for every $t>0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$B/A=e^{\delta t}$$

There is no additive $+1$ on the right-hand side.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Equal starts and $\delta\neq 0$ prevent any later crossing.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$e^{\delta t}\to\infty$ when $\delta>0$, so the factor $B/A$ is arbitrarily large.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$\ln B-\ln A=\delta t$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The raw gap $B-A$ is not linear in $t$ with slope $\delta$; log-gap is.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Equal starts cancel, leaving pure gap factor $e^{\delta t}$. Leadership is decided by the sign of $\delta$; raw level gaps are not the force gap.

tasks.title: Compound claims linking discrete and continuous letters
tasks.context: A portfolio may be viewed either as $P_0(1+b)^{t}$ with $b>-1$ or as $P_0 e^{at}$ with $a=\ln(1+b)$. Claims combine both spellings. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.12$, $b=0.10$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: With $a=\ln(1+b)$, the two spellings define the same function only at integer $t$.
With $a=\ln(1+b)$, doubling time is not $\dfrac{\ln 2}{b}$ whenever $b\neq\ln(1+b)$.
For $b>0$, matching continuous force is strictly smaller than the discrete net rate $b$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$P_0(1+b)^{t}=P_0 e^{t\ln(1+b)}$$

The identity holds for every real $t$, not merely integers.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Doubling uses denominator $a=\ln(1+b)$. Since $\ln(1+b)\neq b$ for $b\neq 0$, the time is not $\ln 2/b$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$T=\frac{\ln 2}{a}=\frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+b)}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Since $\ln(1+b)<b$ for $b>0$, the reciprocal reverses the inequality, yielding $\ln 2/\ln(1+b)>\ln 2/b$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$\ln(1+b)<b\quad(b>0)$$

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Identify $a=\ln(1+b)$ to unify spellings. Doubling is $\ln 2/\ln(1+b)$, which exceeds the naive $\ln 2/b$ because $\ln(1+b)<b$.

tasks.title: Policy switch raising force after letter $T$
tasks.context: Capital grows at force $a_1$ until a reform date $T>0$, then at a higher force $a_2>a_1$: the standard piecewise continuous-exponential definition applies with letters $P_0>0$, $a_1$, $a_2$, $T$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.07$, initial level $400$, horizon $T=15$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Ignoring the reform and using force $a_1$ forever understates $P(t)$ for every $t>T$.
For every $t>T$, the true path strictly exceeds the constant-$a_1$ extrapolation from time $0$.
At $t=T$, both the true path and the no-reform path agree.
The true path after $T$ equals $P_0 e^{a_2 t}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

After $T$ the true force $a_2>a_1$ is larger, so the no-reform path lies strictly below the true path.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$P_0 e^{a_1 T}e^{a_2(t-T)}>P_0 e^{a_1 t}\iff a_2(t-T)>a_1(t-T)$$

which holds because $a_2>a_1$ and $t>T$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Both paths equal $P_0 e^{a_1 T}$ at the switch.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

That formula would apply only if force $a_2$ had been used from time $0$. The early window still used $a_1$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

That is exactly the second piece of the definition.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Match at $T$, then apply $a_2$. Constant-$a_1$ extrapolation understates post-reform levels when $a_2>a_1$. Do not pretend $a_2$ applied from time zero.

tasks.title: Applied Newton — ambient $T_a$ and force $b$ as letters
tasks.context: Coffee cools in a room at ambient letter $T_a$ according to $T(t)=T_a+(T_0-T_a)e^{-bt}$ with $T_0>T_a$ and $b>0$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.05$, $b=0.04$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The time to the midpoint $\dfrac{T_0+T_a}{2}$ equals $\dfrac{\ln 2}{b}$.
Raising $b$ shortens every hitting time to a fixed interior target between $T_a$ and $T_0$.
Raising $T_a$ while holding $T_0,b$ fixed leaves all hitting times to levels above the old $T_a$ unchanged.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The gap factor $e^{-bt}\in(0,1)$ for $t>0$ keeps $T(t)$ strictly between $T_a$ and $T_0$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The gap stays positive, so $T(t)$ approaches $T_a$ from above and never crosses it.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Midpoint means the gap has halved:

$$e^{-bt}=\frac12\implies t=\frac{\ln 2}{b}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Hitting-time formulas have $1/b$ in front; larger $b$ shortens times.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Changing ambient reshapes every gap $T_\ast-T_a$, so hitting times move.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Cooling stays trapped between $T_0$ and $T_a$. Half-gap time is $\ln 2/b$. Force scales all clocks; ambient shifts targets.

tasks.title: Graph comparison — force $a$ versus factor $1+b$
tasks.context: The figure sketches $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$ against $Q(t)=P_0(1+b)^{t}$ for one positive pair with $e^{a}\neq 1+b$. Interpret claims in letters $P_0>0$, $a$, $b>-1$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.06$, $b=0.05$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Both paths share the same initial value $P_0$.
The discrete path lies strictly below the continuous path whenever $b=a>0$.
With fixed unequal multipliers, the two paths cannot touch at three distinct positive times.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\frac{P}{Q}=e^{(a-\ln(1+b))t}$$

When $a>\ln(1+b)$ and $t>0$ the ratio exceeds $1$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Both formulas give $P_0$ at $t=0$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

For $b=a>0$ one has $e^{a}>1+a$, so continuous lies above discrete for $t>0$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Log-gap is linear in $t$, so agreement occurs at most at $t=0$ unless multipliers match (in which case they agree everywhere).

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$\ln P-\ln Q=\bigl(a-\ln(1+b)\bigr)t$$

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Compare via $P/Q=\exp\bigl((a-\ln(1+b))t\bigr)$. Shared start; at most one agreement time unless forces match. For $b=a>0$ continuous wins.

tasks.title: Recover discrete letter $b$ from a geometric table
tasks.context: A balance follows exact discrete compounding $Q(t)=Q_0(1+b)^{t}$ on the integer grid, with letters $Q_0>0$ and $b>-1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The one-year growth rate in percent is $100(1+b)$ (as a letter expression).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$1+b=\frac{Q(1)}{Q(0)}\implies b=\frac{Q(1)}{Q(0)}-1$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$a=\ln(1+b)=\ln\frac{Q(1)}{Q(0)}$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Only in the knife-edge $b=0$ does $a=b$; generally $a=\ln(1+b)\neq b$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

$$\frac{Q(3)}{Q(1)}=(1+b)^{2}$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The net one-year rate is $b$, so the percent expression is $100b$, not $100(1+b)$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Read $1+b$ from the first ratio; convert to continuous force by a logarithm. Multi-year ratios are powers of $1+b$.

tasks.title: Ordering continuous forces without numeric drills
tasks.context: Three continuous-exponential paths share the same $P_0>0$ but use forces $a_1<a_2<a_3$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.04$, $b=0.03$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $t>0$, $P_0 e^{a_1 t}<P_0 e^{a_2 t}<P_0 e^{a_3 t}$.
Semi-log slopes increase strictly in the index $b$.
If each force is replaced by its negative, then for every $t>0$ one has $P_0 e^{-a_1 t}>P_0 e^{-a_2 t}>P_0 e^{-a_3 t}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The map $a\mapsto e^{at}$ is increasing for each fixed $t>0$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Larger force shortens doubling time, so $T_1>T_2>T_3$, not the claimed increasing order.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

$$T_b=\frac{\ln 2}{a_b}$$

hence $a_1<a_2<a_3$ implies $T_1>T_2>T_3$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Semi-log slope equals the force, so slopes inherit $a_1<a_2<a_3$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Negating reverses the order of forces, and therefore reverses the order of levels at each $t>0$.

$$e^{-a_1 t}>e^{-a_2 t}>e^{-a_3 t}$$

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Larger force raises every positive-time level and steepens semi-log slope, but shortens doubling time. Negating all forces reverses which index leads.

tasks.title: Parametric family $P_c(t)=P_0 e^{c t}$
tasks.context: Index a family of paths by a force letter $c\in\mathbb{R}$: $P_c(t)=P_0 e^{c t}$ with fixed $P_0>0$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $c=0.05$, $d=0.08$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For each fixed $t>0$, $c\mapsto P_c(t)$ is strictly increasing.
$P_c$ coincides with $P_d$ as functions on $\mathbb{R}$ if and only if $c=d$.
$P_c(t)=P_{-c}(-t)$ holds for every real $c$ and every real $t$.
The map $c\mapsto T_2(c)=\dfrac{\ln 2}{c}$ (for $c>0$) is strictly decreasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\partial_c P_c(t)=t P_0 e^{c t}>0\quad(t>0)$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

If $c\neqd$ then already at $t=1$ the values $P_0 e^{c}$ and $P_0 e^{d}$ differ.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$P_0 e^{c t}=P_0 e^{(-c)(-t)}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$e^{2}=e^{(-1)\cdot(-2)}$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

As $c$ rises, $\ln 2/c$ falls.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Force indexes the family injectively. Time reversal pairs $c$ with $-c$. Doubling time decreases in $c$.

tasks.title: Rebuild from one point and a calibrated force
tasks.context: A continuous-exponential path has known force $a$ and passes through a single observation $(t_\ast,P_\ast)$ with $P_\ast>0$. Rebuild $P(t)$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.07$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The implied initial level is $P_0=P_\ast e^{-a t_\ast}$.
Doubling time (if $a>0$) remains $\dfrac{\ln 2}{a}$, independent of the observation.
The observation alone, without $a$, does not determine the entire path.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$P(t)=P_\ast e^{a(t-t_\ast)}$$

The anchor shift is $t-t_\ast$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

Omitting the time shift would force the observation to lie at $t=0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

$$P_0=P(0)=P_\ast e^{-a t_\ast}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Doubling depends only on force, not on where the path was observed.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

One point leaves a one-parameter family; the force letter is required to pin $a$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Anchor at the observation: $P(t)=P_\ast e^{a(t-t_\ast)}$. Back out $P_0$ if needed. Characteristic times still depend only on $a$.

tasks.title: Nested $\ln$ of a continuous path
tasks.context: Let $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$ with $P_0>0$. Compare single and double logarithms of the path. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.05$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: There exist $P_0>e$ and $a>0$ such that $\ln\ln P(t)$ is defined for all large $t$ yet $\ln\ln P(t)\neq at$ for some such $t$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+at$$

Logs turn products into sums, not products of the log pieces.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$\ln(e^{at})=at$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

$$\ln\ln P(t)=\ln(\ln P_0+at)$$

This equals $at$ only in nongeneric cases, not for every $P_0>e$ and every $t\ge 0$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Take $P_0=e^{2}$ and $a=1$. Then $\ln\ln P(t)=\ln(2+t)$, which differs from $t$ at $t=1$ since $\ln 3\neq 1$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

$$e^{\ln P+at}=P e^{at}=P_0 e^{2at}$$

$$P^{2}=P_0^{2} e^{2at}$$

Equality for every $t$ forces $P_0=1$, contradicting universality over every $P_0>0$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Single logs linearise continuous exponentials. Double logs produce $\ln(\ln P_0+at)$, not $at$. Algebraic slips with $e^{\ln P+at}$ introduce extra factors.

tasks.title: Hybrid semi-log table — slope letter $a$
tasks.context: The table lists exact log-levels of $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$. The figure sketches the semi-log geometry for one positive pair. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The chord from $t=0$ to $t=4$ has slope $4a$.
The chord from $t=2$ to $t=4$ has slope $a$.
The table is inconsistent with force $2a$ in place of $a$.
Exponentiating the middle entry recovers $P(2)=P_0 e^{2a}$.
If $a<0$, the semi-log plot slopes upward.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\frac{4a}{4}=a$$

The chord slope equals $a$, not $4a$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$\frac{(\ln P_0+4a)-(\ln P_0+2a)}{2}=a$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Force $2a$ would produce increments $4a$ and $8a$ over those windows, contradicting the table.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$P(2)=e^{\ln P_0+2a}=P_0 e^{2a}$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Negative $a$ yields a downward semi-log slope.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Every chord on $\ln P=\ln P_0+at$ returns slope $a$. Exponentiate to recover levels. Sign of $a$ is the sign of the semi-log slope.

tasks.title: Precisely-when criteria for exponential structure
tasks.context: Let $P:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be differentiable. Consider criteria that characterise continuous-exponential form $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.08$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $P'/P$ constant on $(0,\infty)$ if and only if $P$ is continuous-exponential.
$\ln P$ affine on $(0,\infty)$ if and only if $P$ is continuous-exponential.
$P''>0$ everywhere does not by itself characterise continuous-exponential structure.
Constant successive ratios on every pair of times distance $1$ apart are necessary for continuous-exponential structure.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The ODE $P'=aP$ with $P>0$ integrates to $P(t)=Ce^{at}$. Conversely every continuous exponential has constant relative rate.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Affinity of $\ln P$ is the integrated form of the same criterion.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Strict convexity holds for many non-exponential positives (e.g. $t^{2}+1$ on $(0,\infty)$).

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Continuous exponentials have $P(t+1)/P(t)=e^{a}$ constantly — necessity holds.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Integrate from the anchor $t=1$ to obtain that shifted formula.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Constant relative rate, or affine log, characterises continuous exponentials. Convexity is weaker. Unit-lag ratios are constant for this class.

tasks.title: Average force across a piecewise exponential
tasks.context: Take the piecewise path with forces $a_1$ on $[0,T]$ and $a_2$ on $(T,t_\bullet]$ for a horizon $t_\bullet>T$, starting at $P_0>0$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.04$, horizon $T=12$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The average force on $[0,t_\bullet]$ equals $a_1 T+a_2(t_\bullet-T)$ without dividing by $t_\bullet$.
That average depends on $T$ and $t_\bullet$ in general, not merely on $(a_1+a_2)/2$.
Average force equals the arithmetic mean of the endpoint relative rates $\tfrac12\bigl(P'(0)/P(0)+P'(t_\bullet)/P(t_\bullet)\bigr)$ even when $a_1\neq a_2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\frac{a_1 T+a_2(t_\bullet-T)}{t_\bullet}$$

Average force divides the accumulated log growth by elapsed time.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Weights are the time spent in each regime; they need not be equal half-and-half, so the average is not automatically $(a_1+a_2)/2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Chain the two exponential pieces to obtain that product of factors.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Equal forces make the weighted average equal to the common force.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Endpoint relative rates are $a_1$ and $a_2$, whose arithmetic mean ignores time weights and generally differs from the duration-weighted average.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Average force is duration-weighted: $(a_1 T+a_2(t_\bullet-T))/t_\bullet$. It equals the plain mean of endpoint forces only in symmetric special cases.

tasks.title: Applied — when per capita force vanishes
tasks.context: Output and population forces are letters $a$ and $b$. Per capita is $c=Y/N$ with the usual continuous-exponential aggregates. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.12$, $b=0.10$, $c=0.05$, initial level $1200$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $c$ is constant for every choice of $a,b$.
If $a=b$, then $Y$ and $N$ share the same continuous force.
If $a=b$, then $Y(t)=N(t)$ for every $t$ need not hold without $Y_0=N_0$ in comparable units.
The claim '$c$ grows because both $Y$ and $N$ grow' is not warranted without comparing $a$ and $b$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Constancy requires $a=b$; it is not automatic for arbitrary letters.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$a-b=0\iff a=b$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Same force letter means both aggregates use that common rate.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Equal forces preserve the ratio $Y/N$, but the levels themselves need not coincide.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Both growing is compatible with falling per capita when $b>a$. The comparison is essential.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Per capita freezes iff $a=b$. Equal forces do not equate levels. Growth of both aggregates does not imply growth of the ratio.

tasks.title: Semi-log decay graph — reading negative calibrated force
tasks.context: The figure illustrates $\ln P$ for a decaying continuous exponential $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$ with $a<0$. Claims use the letter $a$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.07$, $d=0.09$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The semi-log slope equals $|a|$ (unsigned) even when $a<0$.
Half-life does not equal $\dfrac{\ln 2}{a}$ when $a<0$, because that expression is negative.
On the semi-log plot, equal horizontal steps produce equal vertical drops.
Because the semi-log plot is linear, the raw $P$-plot is also linear.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\frac{d}{dt}\ln P=a$$

Slope carries the signed force $a$, which is negative in decay.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Half-life must be positive; the correct formula uses $|a|$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$T_{1/2}=\frac{\ln 2}{|a|}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Linearity of $\ln P$ means constant slope, hence equal run produces equal rise/drop.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Linearity after logs still leaves an exponential in the original level.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Negative semi-log slope is the force $a<0$. Half-life uses $|a|$. Equal steps on a line give equal log drops; raw levels stay curved.

tasks.title: Table that breaks pure exponential structure
tasks.context: A proposed table for a positive series is shown below in letters $P_0>0$ and $a\neq 0$. Decide whether a pure continuous exponential can generate it. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.05$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The successive ratios $P(1)/P(0)$ and $P(2)/P(1)$ are equal for every $a\neq 0$.
The successive ratios disagree only when $a=0$.
No choice of force makes this table a sampling of $P_0 e^{at}$ at $t=0,1,2$.
Replacing the $t=2$ entry by $P_0 e^{2a}$ would restore pure continuous-exponential structure.
The displayed $t=2$ entry equals $P_0 e^{2a}$ for every $a$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\frac{P(1)}{P(0)}=e^{a}$$

$$\frac{P(2)}{P(1)}=\frac{e^{a}+e^{2a}}{e^{a}}=1+e^{a}$$

These are unequal for every real $a$, so the universal equality claim is false.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

The ratios $e^{a}$ and $1+e^{a}$ disagree for every real $a$, including $a\neq 0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Pure continuous exponentials need constant ratios; this table lacks them.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The corrected triple $(P_0,P_0 e^{a},P_0 e^{2a})$ is exactly the exponential sample.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

$$P_0 e^{a}+P_0 e^{2a}=P_0 e^{2a}\iff e^{a}=0$$

which never holds, so the displayed entry is not $P_0 e^{2a}$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Compare successive ratios. The given $t=2$ entry spoils constancy, so the table is not pure exponential; correcting it to $P_0 e^{2a}$ restores the model.

tasks.title: Batch of continuous-exponential algebraic identities
tasks.context: Assume $P(t)=P_0 e^{at}$ with $P_0>0$. Treat $a,t,c$ as real letters. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.06$, $b=0.05$, $c=0.025$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $P(t)+P(c)=P(t+c)$ fails for some $t,c$ (exponentials are not additive).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$P(t+c)=P_0 e^{a(t+c)}=P(t)e^{ac}$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$P(t)P(c)=P_0^{2} e^{a(t+c)}=P_0\cdot P(t+c)$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$\frac{P(t)}{P(c)}=e^{a(t-c)}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Exponentials satisfy multiplicative Cauchy laws, not additive ones. For $t=c=1$, $2P_0 e^{a}\neq P_0 e^{2a}$ whenever $e^{a}\neq 2$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$\bigl(P(t)/P_0\bigr)^{b}=e^{knt}=P(bt)/P_0$$

hence $P(bt)=P_0(P(t)/P_0)^{b}$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Continuous exponentials are multiplicative in time shifts. Products introduce an extra $P_0$; sums do not recombine into $P(t+c)$.

tasks.title: Parametric mix — capital, labour, and per-worker output
tasks.context: In a lettered Solow-style sketch, capital-like output $Y=Y_0 e^{at}$ and labour $N=N_0 e^{bt}$ yield per-worker output $c=Y/N$. Forces $a,b$ are letters; no huge numeric GDP figures appear. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.08$, $b=0.07$, $c=0.03$, initial level $800$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Per-worker force is not the product $ab$.
If $a>b$, per-worker output is strictly increasing.
If $a>0$, per-worker output is strictly increasing regardless of $b$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$c=c_0 e^{(a-b)t}$$

The force is the difference $a-b$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Log-ratios differentiate to a difference of forces, never a product $ab$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Force $a-b>0$ makes $c$ strictly increasing.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A large population force can dominate a positive $a$ and drive $c$ down.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

$$T=\frac{\ln 2}{a-b}$$

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Close with the difference force $a-b$: monotonicity and doubling time both read off $a-b$, never a product $ab$, and never $a$ alone.

tasks.title: Two concrete forces — continuous vs discrete mismatch
tasks.context: A fund starts at $P_0=1000$. Path $P$ uses continuous force $a=0.05$, so $P(t)=1000\,e^{0.05 t}$. Path $Q$ uses annual factor $1+b$ with $b=0.05$, so $Q(t)=1000(1.05)^t$. Note that $e^{0.05}\neq 1.05$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If the discrete factor were changed to $e^{0.05}$, then $P$ and $Q$ would coincide for every $t\ge 0$.
The continuous doubling time is $T=\dfrac{\ln 2}{0.05}$, independent of the initial $1000$.
Replacing $e^{0.05 t}$ by $(1.05)^t$ leaves every level $P(t)$ unchanged.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Under continuous force $0.05$, one year multiplies by $e^{0.05}$, not by $1.05$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Since $e^{0.05}>1.05$, we get $P(1)=1000 e^{0.05}>1000\cdot 1.05=Q(1)$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Matching one-year factors forces $P\equiv Q$ for all $t$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Solve $e^{0.05 T}=2$ to get $T=(\ln 2)/0.05$; $P_0$ cancels.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Because $e^{0.05}\neq 1.05$, the paths diverge for $t>0$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Compare $e^{0.05}$ with $1.05$, then read off doubling and path identity.

tasks.title: Table recovery with concrete levels — force identity traps
tasks.context: A continuous exponential $P(t)=P_0 e^{a t}$ produces the exact sample $P(0)=800$, $P(2)=800 e^{0.2}$, $P(4)=800 e^{0.4}$. No rounding. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The average relative growth from $t=0$ to $t=4$ equals the force $a$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

From $P(2)/P(0)=e^{2a}=e^{0.2}$ we get $2a=0.2$, hence $a=0.1$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Directly from the given sample.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Ratios over equal steps are equal: $P(4)/P(2)=e^{0.2}=P(2)/P(0)$, not twice that.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Extrapolating $P(t)=800 e^{0.1 t}$ yields $P(6)=800 e^{0.6}$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Average relative growth over $[0,4]$ is $(e^{0.4}-1)/4$, which is not equal to $a=0.1$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Recover $a$ from equal-step ratios; reject confusing average growth with force.

tasks.title: Piecewise concrete forces — average force is not automatic midpoint
tasks.context: A balance starts at $2000$. It grows at continuous force $a=0.06$ on $[0,5]$ and then at force $b=0.02$ on $(5,10]$. Let $A(10)$ be the terminal level. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The constant force $\bar a$ that yields the same $A(10)$ in one shot equals $0.04$.
The arithmetic mean $\dfrac{a+b}{2}$ equals that constant force $\bar a$ here because both intervals last $5$ years.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

On $[0,5]$: $A(5)=2000 e^{0.06\cdot 5}=2000 e^{0.3}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Then five more years at $0.02$ multiply by $e^{0.1}$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Need $e^{10\bar a}=e^{0.4}$, so $\bar a=0.04$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$(0.06+0.02)/2=0.04=\bar a$ in this equal-duration case.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Using $0.06$ for the whole decade ignores the switch to $0.02$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Multiply piecewise factors; compare time-average force with a naive single rate.

tasks.title: GDP per capita with concrete growth rates
tasks.context: Aggregate output $Y(t)=Y_0 e^{0.03 t}$ and population $N(t)=N_0 e^{0.01 t}$ with $Y_0=500$, $N_0=25$. Per-capita output is $d=Y/N$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If population force rose to $0.03$, per-capita output would be constant in $t$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$d(0)=500/25=20$ and force $0.03-0.01=0.02$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Quotient rule for exponential forces.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The correct simplification is $20 e^{(0.03-0.01)t}=20 e^{0.02 t}$, not $e^{0.04 t}$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Solve $e^{0.02 T}=2$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Forces cancel when both equal $0.03$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Per-capita force is the difference of log-derivatives.

tasks.title: Discrete compounding ladder with concrete steps
tasks.context: A deposit of $1200$ compounds once per year at rate $b=0.08$, so $Q(t)=1200(1.08)^t$. A continuous rival uses force $a$ with $e^{a}=1.08$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The continuous rival $P(t)=1200 e^{a t}$ satisfies $P(t)=Q(t)$ for every $t\ge 0$.
After one year both models multiply the deposit by $1.08$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

By construction $e^{a}=1.08$ forces $a=\ln 1.08$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Direct evaluation of the discrete formula.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Matching one-year factors makes the paths identical.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

$\ln 1.08\neq 0.08$; the force is the log of the factor.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Both one-year multipliers equal $1.08$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Match discrete factor to continuous force via $a=\ln(1+b)$.

tasks.title: Cooling law with concrete ambient data
tasks.context: Newton cooling: $T(t)=20+80 e^{-0.2 t}$ (ambient $20$, initial $100$). Time is in minutes. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The half-life of the gap $T(t)-20$ equals $5$ minutes.
The half-life of the gap $T(t)-20$ is $\dfrac{\ln 2}{0.2}$.

tasks.solution_overview: Quotient law is fine; dividing logs is not; change-of-base is a different statement.

tasks.title: Final tangle: domain of $\log(b-x)+\log(x-a)$ versus the product form
tasks.context: Let $a<b$ and compare $$c(x)=\log(b-x)+\log(x-a)$$ with $$d(x)=\log\bigl((b-x)(x-a)\bigr)$$ for base $>1$. Concrete parameter values (statements still hinge on identities / comparisons, not on reading a single substituted number): $a=0.04$, $b=0.03$, $c=0.01$, $d=0.02$. Evaluate each statement. statements: $d$ could in principle be defined where the product is positive even if a factor is negative, but with two linear factors and $a<b$ that still forces $(a,b)$.
$c$ requires each factor positive separately, so its domain cannot exceed $(a,b)$.
Nested logarithms are defined for every $x>0$ without further checks.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Each factor positive iff $x\in(a,b)$; product positive on the same interval.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Product law on $(a,b)$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

For this quadratic opening downward, positivity is exactly $(a,b)$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Sum of logs needs both arguments positive.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Each outer log still needs a positive inner value.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: For $a<b$, sum and product forms share domain $(a,b)$ and agree there.

tasks.title: Change-of-base with concrete logs
tasks.context: Use $\ln 2\approx 0.693$, $\ln 3\approx 1.099$, $\ln 5\approx 1.609$ as given reference values (treat them as exact for this exercise). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

tasks.title: Domain of a concrete log product
tasks.context: Consider the real function $\ln\bigl((x-1)(4-x)\bigr)$ (no extra named map beyond the expression itself). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

tasks.title: Solving a concrete exponential via logs

tasks.title: Elasticities from a concrete log demand
